beats.narration_text: Mingalaba. This is Liam, in for Bear, with a short film for INFO seventy-three seventy-five, Branding and AI. You might think a polished portfolio proves what you can do. It only proves something if it cost you something to make.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. A signal: something you show that stands in for what others can't see. A costly signal: one that's hard to fake cheaply, so it tells people apart. And pooling: when everyone can produce the signal, so it stops telling anyone apart.

hard to fake cheaply, so it tells people apart
everyone can produce the signal, so it stops sorting

beats.narration_text: In 1973, the economist Michael Spence asked a simple question. An employer wants productive people, but you can't see productivity until after the hire. So how does anyone choose?

shot.visual_intent: Five sealed kraft boxes drop onto the stage in a row; a grey bracket draws over them ('can't see inside').

beats.narration_text: They look at signals: things you can show that stand in for what they can't see. Spence's example was a degree.

shot.visual_intent: White page tags drop onto two of the five boxes ('signal').

beats.narration_text: A degree works as a signal because it's costly, and costlier for some people than for others. It's hard to fake cheaply, so it tells people apart.

shot.visual_intent: A staircase of kraft steps builds; two small boxes climb it; one reaches the top and gets a page tag, the other stops halfway ('costly').
shot.motion_claim: A staircase of kraft steps builds; two small boxes climb it; one reaches the top and gets a page tag, the other stops halfway ('costly').

beats.narration_text: When the cost holds, the signal separates people. Spence called that a separating equilibrium. The work later shared a Nobel prize, for markets where one side knows more than the other.

shot.visual_intent: A grey sorter splits into two lanes; boxes with tags slide into the right lane, boxes without into the left ('separating').

beats.narration_text: Now AI has made some of those signals nearly free. A working demo app. A clean cover letter. A polished essay, a logo, a slide deck. In one experiment, programmers with an AI assistant built a small web server in less than half the time.

shot.visual_intent: A dark server stack lights up and prints page tags, one after another, onto every box in the row ('AI').
shot.motion_claim: A dark server stack lights up and prints page tags, one after another, onto every box in the row ('AI').

beats.narration_text: When everyone can produce the signal, it stops sorting. Spence called that pooling. Everyone looks the same on paper, and the employer is back to guessing.

shot.visual_intent: The two lanes merge into one; every tagged box slides into the same pile ('pooling').
shot.motion_claim: The two lanes merge into one; every tagged box slides into the same pile ('pooling').

beats.narration_text: So what didn't get cheap? Judgment: choosing what's worth making. Ideation: finding a problem real people actually have. Creative taste. And the effort of putting something in front of real users and changing it because of what they said. Those still cost you something, so they still signal.

shot.visual_intent: In the pooled pile, one box lifts out and gets the terracotta tape; three dots light beside it one by one ('judgment').

beats.narration_text: So show the expensive part. The problem you chose, and why. The versions you threw away. What real users told you, and what you changed. The artifact is cheap now. The reasons behind it aren't.

shot.visual_intent: The taped box opens; three white pages rise out of it and fan to the right ('why', 'versions', 'users').

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick one project you'd show an employer, and paste this into Claude: Here's a project in my portfolio: describe it. Act as a skeptical hiring manager who knows AI can produce code and text cheaply. Tell me which parts of this project an AI could have made in an afternoon, and which parts show judgment an AI couldn't supply. Then suggest three things I could add so the costly part is visible to a stranger. Then check two things yourself. Is each costly part something you actually did? And could a stranger see it without asking you?
